concepts.label: What Is Alive: Why Molecules Must Keep Moving
concepts.cardText: We tend to think of movement, growth-related or not, as evidence for being alive. But a plant that is not visibly growing is still alive, and some animals can breathe without visible movement, so visible movement is not enough to define life. Movements over very small scales, such as movements of molecules, are invisible to the naked eye, and biologists say this molecular movement is necessary for life. Living organisms are well-organised structures: tissues, cells, and smaller components. Because of the effects of the environment, this ordered nature is very likely to keep breaking down over time, and if order breaks down the organism will no longer be alive. So living creatures must keep repairing and maintaining their structures. Since these structures are made of molecules, they must move molecules around all the time.

concepts.label: Life Processes: Nutrition, Respiration, Transport and Excretion
concepts.cardText: The maintenance functions of living organisms must go on even when they are not doing anything particular, even when we are asleep. The processes which together perform this maintenance job are life processes. Since they are needed to prevent damage and break-down, energy is needed, and this energy comes from outside the body in the form of food; the process of taking food from outside to inside is called nutrition. Raw material from outside is also needed for the body to grow. Food sources are converted to a uniform source of energy through chemical reactions, and acquiring oxygen from outside and using it to break down food for cellular needs is respiration. Food and oxygen must be carried around the body, which needs a transportation system, and the waste by-products of these reactions must be removed by a process called excretion.

concepts.label: Single-celled and Multi-cellular Organisms: Why Diffusion Is Not Enough
concepts.cardText: In a single-celled organism no specific organs for taking in food, exchange of gases or removal of wastes may be needed, because the entire surface of the organism is in contact with the environment. But when the body size increases and the design becomes more complex, in multi-cellular organisms all the cells may not be in direct contact with the surrounding environment. Thus simple diffusion will not meet the requirements of all the cells. The uptake of food and oxygen becomes the function of specialised tissues, but then food and oxygen are taken up at one place while all parts of the body need them. This creates the need for a transportation system, and a specialised tissue for excretion will also develop.

concepts.label: Autotrophs and Heterotrophs
concepts.cardText: When we walk or ride a bicycle we use up energy, and even when we are not doing any apparent activity, energy is needed to maintain a state of order in our body. We also need materials from outside to grow, develop and synthesise protein and other substances. This source of energy and materials is the food we eat. The general requirement is common in all organisms but is fulfilled in different ways. Some organisms use simple food material obtained from inorganic sources in the form of carbon dioxide and water; these organisms, the autotrophs, include green plants and some bacteria. Other organisms utilise complex substances that have to be broken down into simpler ones using bio-catalysts called enzymes. The survival of these heterotrophs depends directly or indirectly on autotrophs. Heterotrophic organisms include animals and fungi.

concepts.label: Photosynthesis: Raw Materials, Chlorophyll and Stored Starch
concepts.cardText: Carbon and energy requirements of autotrophic organisms are fulfilled by photosynthesis. It is the process by which autotrophs take in substances from outside and convert them into stored forms of energy. Carbon dioxide and water are converted into carbohydrates in the presence of sunlight and chlorophyll. Carbohydrates are used for energy by the plant, and those not used immediately are stored as starch, the internal energy reserve; in us some energy derived from food is stored as glycogen. Green dots seen in cells of a leaf cross-section are cell organelles called chloroplasts, which contain chlorophyll. In the variegated leaf activity, only the green parts that contain chlorophyll show starch, so chlorophyll is essential for photosynthesis.

concepts.label: Stomata, Guard Cells and Raw Materials from the Soil
concepts.cardText: Stomata are tiny pores on the surface of leaves through which massive amounts of gaseous exchange take place for photosynthesis. Exchange of gases also occurs across the surface of stems, roots and leaves. Since large amounts of water can also be lost through stomata, the plant closes these pores when it does not need carbon dioxide for photosynthesis. The opening and closing of the pore is a function of the guard cells: the guard cells swell when water flows into them, causing the stomatal pore to open, and the pore closes if the guard cells shrink. Water used in photosynthesis is taken up from the soil by the roots in terrestrial plants. Other materials like nitrogen, phosphorus, iron and magnesium are also taken up from the soil. Nitrogen is an essential element used in the synthesis of proteins and other compounds, taken up as inorganic nitrates or nitrites, or as organic compounds prepared by bacteria from atmospheric nitrogen.

concepts.label: Heterotrophic Nutrition Strategies: Saprophytes, Parasites and Others
concepts.cardText: Each organism is adapted to its environment. The form of nutrition differs depending on the type and availability of food material as well as how it is obtained by the organism; for example, whether the food source is stationary, such as grass, or mobile, such as a deer, allows for differences in how food is accessed, as between a cow and a lion. Some organisms break down the food material outside the body and then absorb it; examples are fungi like bread moulds, yeast and mushrooms. Others take in whole material and break it down inside their bodies, depending on body design and functioning. Some other organisms derive nutrition from plants or animals without killing them; this parasitic nutritive strategy is used by cuscuta (amar-bel), ticks, lice, leeches and tape-worms.

concepts.label: Nutrition in Amoeba and Paramoecium
concepts.cardText: Since the food and the way it is obtained differ, the digestive system is different in various organisms. In single-celled organisms the food may be taken in by the entire surface. Amoeba takes in food using temporary finger-like extensions of the cell surface which fuse over the food particle forming a food-vacuole. Inside the food-vacuole, complex substances are broken down into simpler ones which then diffuse into the cytoplasm, and the remaining undigested material is moved to the surface of the cell and thrown out. In Paramoecium, also a unicellular organism, the cell has a definite shape and food is taken in at a specific spot, to which it is moved by the movement of cilia which cover the entire surface of the cell.

concepts.label: Digestion in the Mouth: Teeth, Saliva and Peristalsis
concepts.cardText: The alimentary canal is basically a long tube extending from the mouth to the anus, with regions specialised for different functions. Food is first crushed by the teeth to generate small particles of the same texture, and it is wetted so its passage through the soft lining is smooth. When we eat something we like, our mouth waters; this is not only water but a fluid called saliva secreted by the salivary glands. Complex food must be broken into smaller molecules to be absorbed, which is done with the help of biological catalysts called enzymes. Saliva contains the enzyme salivary amylase, which breaks down starch, a complex molecule, to give simple sugar. The muscular tongue mixes the food with saliva. The lining of the canal has muscles that contract rhythmically to push the food forward; these peristaltic movements occur all along the gut.

concepts.label: Digestion in the Stomach
concepts.cardText: From the mouth the food is taken to the stomach through the food-pipe or oesophagus. The stomach is a large organ which expands when food enters it, and its muscular walls help in mixing the food thoroughly with more digestive juices. Digestion in the stomach is taken care of by the gastric glands present in its wall, which release hydrochloric acid, a protein digesting enzyme called pepsin, and mucus. The hydrochloric acid creates an acidic medium which facilitates the action of the enzyme pepsin. The mucus protects the inner lining of the stomach from the action of the acid under normal conditions. The exit of food from the stomach is regulated by a sphincter muscle which releases it in small amounts into the small intestine.

concepts.label: The Small Intestine: Bile, Pancreatic Juice and Complete Digestion
concepts.cardText: The small intestine is the longest part of the alimentary canal, fitted into a compact space by extensive coiling, and is the site of the complete digestion of carbohydrates, proteins and fats. It receives the secretions of the liver and pancreas. The food coming from the stomach is acidic and has to be made alkaline for the pancreatic enzymes to act; bile juice from the liver accomplishes this and also acts on fats. Fats are present in the intestine as large globules, which makes it difficult for enzymes to act on them; bile salts break them into smaller globules, increasing the efficiency of enzyme action, similar to the emulsifying action of soaps on dirt. The pancreas secretes pancreatic juice containing trypsin for digesting proteins and lipase for breaking down emulsified fats. The walls of the small intestine secrete intestinal juice whose enzymes finally convert proteins to amino acids, complex carbohydrates into glucose, and fats into fatty acids and glycerol.

concepts.label: Absorption, Villi and the Length of the Small Intestine
concepts.cardText: Digested food is taken up by the walls of the intestine. The inner lining of the small intestine has numerous finger-like projections called villi, which increase the surface area for absorption. The villi are richly supplied with blood vessels which take the absorbed food to each and every cell of the body, where it is utilised for obtaining energy, building up new tissues and the repair of old tissues. The unabsorbed food is sent into the large intestine, whose wall absorbs more water from this material, and the rest is removed from the body via the anus, with the exit regulated by the anal sphincter. The length of the small intestine differs in various animals depending on the food they eat: herbivores eating grass need a longer small intestine to allow the cellulose to be digested, while meat is easier to digest, so carnivores like tigers have a shorter small intestine.

concepts.label: Breakdown of Glucose: Pyruvate and Anaerobic Respiration
concepts.cardText: The food material taken in during nutrition is used in cells to provide energy for various life processes. Diverse organisms do this in different ways: some use oxygen to break down glucose completely into carbon dioxide and water, while some use other pathways that do not involve oxygen. In all cases, the first step is the break-down of glucose, a six-carbon molecule, into a three-carbon molecule called pyruvate. This process takes place in the cytoplasm. Further, the pyruvate may be converted into ethanol and carbon dioxide. This process takes place in yeast during fermentation. Since it takes place in the absence of air (oxygen), it is called anaerobic respiration.

concepts.label: ATP: The Energy Currency of the Cell
concepts.cardText: The energy released during cellular respiration is immediately used to synthesise a molecule called ATP, which is used to fuel all other activities in the cell. In these processes ATP is broken down, giving rise to a fixed amount of energy which can drive the endothermic reactions taking place in the cell. ATP is the energy currency for most cellular processes. The energy released during respiration is used to make an ATP molecule from ADP and inorganic phosphate. Like a battery which can provide energy for many different kinds of uses, ATP can be used in the cells for the contraction of muscles, protein synthesis, conduction of nervous impulses and many other activities.

concepts.label: Gas Exchange in Plants and in Aquatic and Terrestrial Animals
concepts.cardText: Since the aerobic pathway depends on oxygen, aerobic organisms need to ensure sufficient intake of oxygen. Plants exchange gases through stomata, and large inter-cellular spaces ensure that all cells are in contact with air; carbon dioxide and oxygen are exchanged by diffusion, in a direction that depends on the environmental conditions and the requirements of the plant. At night, when there is no photosynthesis, CO2 elimination is the major exchange activity; during the day, CO2 from respiration is used up for photosynthesis, so there is no CO2 release and oxygen release is the major event. Terrestrial animals breathe the oxygen in the atmosphere, but animals that live in water use the oxygen dissolved in water. Since dissolved oxygen is fairly low compared to the oxygen in air, the rate of breathing in aquatic organisms is much faster than in terrestrial organisms. Fishes take in water through their mouths and force it past the gills where the dissolved oxygen is taken up by blood.

concepts.label: The Human Respiratory System
concepts.cardText: Terrestrial organisms use the oxygen in the atmosphere, absorbed by organs that have a structure increasing the surface area in contact with the oxygen-rich atmosphere. This surface is very fine and delicate, so it is placed within the body, with passages that take air to it and a mechanism for moving the air in and out. In human beings, air is taken in through the nostrils, where fine hairs and mucus filter it, then passes through the throat into the lungs; rings of cartilage in the throat ensure that the air passage does not collapse. Within the lungs the passage divides into smaller and smaller tubes which end in balloon-like structures called alveoli, which provide a surface where gases are exchanged and whose walls contain an extensive network of blood vessels. When we breathe in, we lift our ribs and flatten our diaphragm, the chest cavity becomes larger and air is sucked into the lungs. The blood brings carbon dioxide for release into the alveoli and takes up oxygen from the alveolar air. The lungs always contain a residual volume of air so there is sufficient time for oxygen to be absorbed and carbon dioxide released.

concepts.label: Haemoglobin and the Transport of Oxygen and Carbon Dioxide
concepts.cardText: When the body size of animals is large, the diffusion pressure alone cannot take care of oxygen delivery to all parts of the body. Instead, respiratory pigments take up oxygen from the air in the lungs and carry it to tissues which are deficient in oxygen before releasing it. In human beings the respiratory pigment is haemoglobin, which has a very high affinity for oxygen and is present in the red blood corpuscles. Carbon dioxide is more soluble in water than oxygen is, and hence is mostly transported in the dissolved form in our blood. If the alveolar surface were spread out, it would cover about 80 m2, making gas exchange very efficient. If diffusion alone moved oxygen in our body, it is estimated that it would take 3 years for a molecule of oxygen to get from our lungs to our toes.

concepts.label: Blood and the Need for a Transport System
concepts.cardText: Blood transports food, oxygen and waste materials in our bodies. Blood is a fluid connective tissue that consists of a fluid medium called plasma in which the cells are suspended. Plasma transports food, carbon dioxide and nitrogenous wastes in dissolved form, and oxygen is carried by the red blood corpuscles. Many other substances like salts are also transported by the blood. We thus need a pumping organ to push blood around the body, a network of tubes to reach all the tissues, and a system in place to ensure that this network can be repaired if damaged.

concepts.label: The Heart and Double Circulation
concepts.cardText: The heart is a muscular organ about as big as our fist. Because both oxygen and carbon dioxide have to be transported by the blood, the heart has different chambers to prevent oxygen-rich blood from mixing with blood containing carbon dioxide. Oxygen-rich blood from the lungs comes to the left atrium, then the left ventricle, which pumps it to the body; de-oxygenated blood from the body comes to the right atrium, then the right ventricle, which pumps it to the lungs. Ventricles have thicker muscular walls than the atria because they pump blood into various organs, and valves ensure blood does not flow backwards. Separating the two sides allows a highly efficient supply of oxygen, useful in birds and mammals that have high energy needs and constantly use energy to maintain body temperature. Amphibians and many reptiles have three-chambered hearts and tolerate some mixing; fishes have two chambers, so blood goes only once through the heart in one cycle, whereas in other vertebrates it goes through the heart twice, which is known as double circulation.

concepts.label: Blood Vessels and Blood Pressure
concepts.cardText: Arteries are the vessels which carry blood away from the heart to various organs of the body. Since the blood emerges from the heart under high pressure, the arteries have thick, elastic walls. Veins collect the blood from different organs and bring it back to the heart; they do not need thick walls because the blood is no longer under pressure, and instead they have valves that ensure the blood flows only in one direction. On reaching an organ or tissue, the artery divides into smaller and smaller vessels; the smallest vessels have walls which are one-cell thick and are called capillaries, and exchange of material between the blood and surrounding cells takes place across this thin wall. The capillaries join together to form veins. The force that blood exerts against the wall of a vessel is called blood pressure, much greater in arteries than in veins. The normal systolic pressure is about 120 mm of Hg and diastolic pressure is 80 mm of Hg.

concepts.label: Transportation in Plants: Xylem and Phloem
concepts.cardText: For plants, the soil is the nearest and richest source of raw materials like nitrogen, phosphorus and other minerals, which are absorbed by the roots, while energy is made in the chlorophyll-containing leaves. If the distances between soil-contacting organs and chlorophyll-containing organs are small, energy and raw materials can easily diffuse to all parts, but if the distances become large, diffusion will not be sufficient and a proper transportation system is essential. Plants do not move and have a large proportion of dead cells in many tissues, so they have low energy needs and can use relatively slow transport systems, though the distances can be very large in very tall trees. Plant transport systems move energy stores from leaves and raw materials from roots through two independently organised conducting tubes: the xylem moves water and minerals obtained from the soil, and the phloem transports products of photosynthesis from the leaves to other parts of the plant.

concepts.label: Transport of Water: Root Pressure and Transpiration
concepts.cardText: In the xylem, vessels and tracheids of the roots, stems and leaves are interconnected to form a continuous system of water-conducting channels. At the roots, cells in contact with the soil actively take up ions, creating a difference in the concentration of these ions between the root and the soil. Water therefore moves into the root from the soil to eliminate this difference, so there is steady movement of water into the root xylem, creating a column of water that is steadily pushed upwards. However, this pressure by itself is unlikely to be enough to move water over the heights commonly seen in plants. Evaporation of water molecules from the cells of a leaf creates a suction which pulls water from the xylem cells of roots. The loss of water in the form of vapour from the aerial parts of the plant is known as transpiration. Transpiration helps in the absorption and upward movement of water and minerals from roots to leaves and in temperature regulation. The effect of root pressure is more important at night; during the day when the stomata are open, the transpiration pull becomes the major driving force.

concepts.label: Transport of Food: Translocation in Phloem
concepts.cardText: The transport of soluble products of photosynthesis is called translocation and it occurs in the part of the vascular tissue known as phloem. Besides the products of photosynthesis, the phloem transports amino acids and other substances, especially delivered to the storage organs of roots, fruits and seeds and to growing organs. Translocation takes place in the sieve tubes with the help of adjacent companion cells, both in upward and downward directions. Unlike transport in xylem, which can be largely explained by simple physical forces, translocation in phloem is achieved by utilising energy. Material like sucrose is transferred into phloem tissue using energy from ATP. This increases the osmotic pressure of the tissue, causing water to move into it, and this pressure moves the material in the phloem to tissues which have less pressure. This allows the phloem to move material according to the plant's needs; for example, in the spring sugar stored in root or stem tissue would be transported to the buds which need energy to grow.

concepts.label: Excretion and the Human Excretory System
concepts.cardText: We have discussed how organisms get rid of gaseous wastes generated during photosynthesis or respiration. Other metabolic activities generate nitrogenous materials which need to be removed. The biological process involved in the removal of these harmful metabolic wastes from the body is called excretion. Many unicellular organisms remove these wastes by simple diffusion from the body surface into the surrounding water, while complex multi-cellular organisms use specialised organs. The excretory system of human beings includes a pair of kidneys, a pair of ureters, a urinary bladder and a urethra. Kidneys are located in the abdomen, one on either side of the backbone. Urine produced in the kidneys passes through the ureters into the urinary bladder where it is stored until it is released through the urethra. The purpose of making urine is to filter out waste products from the blood; just as CO2 is removed from the blood in the lungs, nitrogenous waste such as urea or uric acid are removed from blood in the kidneys.

concepts.label: The Nephron: Filtration and Reabsorption
concepts.cardText: The basic filtration unit in the kidneys, like in the lungs, is a cluster of very thin-walled blood capillaries. Each capillary cluster in the kidney is associated with the cup-shaped end of a coiled tube called Bowman's capsule that collects the filtrate. Each kidney has large numbers of these filtration units called nephrons packed close together. Some substances in the initial filtrate, such as glucose, amino acids, salts and a major amount of water, are selectively re-absorbed as the urine flows along the tube. The amount of water re-absorbed depends on how much excess water there is in the body and on how much dissolved waste there is to be excreted. In a healthy adult the initial filtrate is about 180 L daily but only a litre or two is excreted, because the remaining filtrate is re-absorbed in the kidney tubules. The urine from each kidney enters the ureter and is stored in the urinary bladder until the expanded bladder leads to the urge to pass it out; as the bladder is muscular and under nervous control, we can usually control the urge to urinate.

concepts.label: Artificial Kidney (Hemodialysis)
concepts.cardText: Kidneys are vital organs for survival. Several factors like infections, injury or restricted blood flow to the kidneys reduce their activity, which leads to accumulation of poisonous wastes in the body and can even lead to death. In case of kidney failure, an artificial kidney can be used. An artificial kidney is a device to remove nitrogenous waste products from the blood through dialysis. Artificial kidneys contain a number of tubes with a semi-permeable lining, suspended in a tank filled with dialysing fluid. This fluid has the same osmotic pressure as blood, except that it is devoid of nitrogenous wastes. The patient's blood is passed through these tubes, and during this passage the waste products from the blood pass into the dialysing fluid by diffusion. The purified blood is pumped back into the patient. This is similar to the function of the kidney, but different since there is no re-absorption involved.

concepts.label: Excretion in Plants
concepts.cardText: Plants use completely different strategies for excretion than those of animals. Oxygen itself can be thought of as a waste product generated during photosynthesis. Plants can get rid of excess water by transpiration. For other wastes, plants use the fact that many of their tissues consist of dead cells and that they can even lose some parts such as leaves. Many plant waste products are stored in cellular vacuoles. Waste products may be stored in leaves that fall off. Other waste products are stored as resins and gums, especially in old xylem. Plants also excrete some waste substances into the soil around them.
